title: Following a Path: Pure Pursuit and Stanley, Where Each Cuts the Curve or Swings Across the Line

questions.question: What does pure pursuit steer towards?
options: The nearest point of the path
A point a lookahead distance ahead on the path
The path's direction at the car
questions.explanation: The steering is that of the arc which passes through a point of the path one lookahead away. The lookahead is the only setting.

questions.question: A short lookahead (0.1 m) crossed the path how often, against a long (1.5 m)?
questions.explanation: With 0.1 m it steers hard at a point just ahead, overshoots and steers hard back. With 1.5 m it comes in gently.

questions.question: Where a straight turned into a circle of radius 3 m, a lookahead of 2.0 m strayed at most:
options: 0.000 m: it is exact on a circle
questions.explanation: The point it chases is already round the bend, so it starts turning early and cuts inside. A lookahead of 0.6 m strayed 0.015 m.

questions.question: At the same bend Stanley strayed at most:
questions.explanation: Stanley steers by the heading error and the offset of the front axle, with no look ahead, so it does not start the turn early.

questions.question: What does the angle atan2(-k e, v) in Stanley do?
options: Points the car at a point ahead on the path
Limits the steering to the car's maximum
Turns the front axle back towards the path, more gently at speed
Slows the car as the error grows
questions.explanation: The correction for an offset e is an angle whose tangent is the gain times the offset over the speed. At a higher speed the same offset gets a smaller angle.

questions.question: Why does the nearest-point search only look forward?
options: A path that passes near itself would make the follower jump back
The path's points are sorted by distance
questions.explanation: On a path that loops close to itself the nearest point overall may be on an earlier part. Searching only ahead of the last match keeps the follower moving on.
